proof:
# A three-eighths centroid bound for four interval fibers

Let C be a convex body in `R x R` whose mixed-integer intersection has
exactly four nonempty integer fibers, each a positive-length interval.
Equip their union S with mixed length. If the actual mixed centroid
g has an integer first coordinate, then every closed ambient halfspace
H containing g satisfies

    mu(S intersect H)>=3 mu(S)/8.                         (1)

In particular g is one deterministic point of S with the OC bound
`1/4` in this four-fiber case. The constant 3/8 in (1) is not asserted
to be sharp. This theorem does not assume that the tested cap crosses
every fiber; wholly captured and wholly excluded fibers are included.

## 1. Exact normalization and width constraints

The four integer indices are consecutive by convexity. Their positive
weights put their integer mean at one of the two interior indices.
An integer translation and, if necessary, reflection put the indices
at `-1,0,1,2` and the integer mean at zero. Translate the continuous
coordinate so the full mixed centroid is `(0,0)`.

For a nonvertical halfspace through this point, an invertible affine
fiber shear and continuous scaling make its margin simply `x>=0`.
These transformations preserve the integer lattice, convexity, and
all cap-to-total length ratios. Write the resulting intervals as
`[l_i,r_i]` with lengths w_i. Their lower endpoints form a convex
sequence and their upper endpoints a concave sequence. The centroid
identities are exactly

    sum_i i w_i=0,
    sum_i w_i(l_i+r_i)=0.

Scale all continuous lengths so that `w_1=1`. The base mean then gives

    (w_-1,w_0,w_1,w_2)=(1+2t,s,1,t).

Concavity of the width sequence gives

    0<t<=1/2,  1+t<=s<=2-t.                               (2)

Put

    M=s+2+3t,
    Q=sum_i w_i^2=s^2+2+4t+5t^2,
    A=r_-1, B=r_0, C=r_1, D=r_2.

The continuous centroid identity becomes

    (1+2t)A+sB+C+tD=Q/2.                                 (3)

Jensen for the concave upper-endpoint sequence, with probability
weights w_i/M and integer mean zero, gives

    B>=Q/(2M)>0.

The convex lower-endpoint sequence likewise gives

    l_0<=-Q/(2M)<0.                                      (4)

Thus the central interval is always properly cut, whatever the
orientation of the original ambient halfspace.

## 2. A width inequality specific to the four balanced fibers

Let `w_max=max(s,1+2t)`. Then

    4Q>=3 w_max M.                                      (5)

If `w_max=s`, the difference is

    4Q-3sM=s^2-(6+9t)s+8+16t+20t^2.

It decreases in s throughout (2); at `s=2-t` it is `30t^2>=0`.
If `w_max=1+2t`, the difference is

    4Q-3(1+2t)M=4s^2-(3+6t)s+2-5t+2t^2.

It increases in s throughout (2); at `s=1+t` it is `3-6t>=0`.
These two calculations prove (5) on the entire feasible region.

## 3. No fiber is wholly captured

Suppose `l_i<0` for all four indices. The cap mass is then
`F=sum_i(r_i)_+`. By (3),

    Q/2=sum_i w_i r_i<=w_max sum_i(r_i)_+=w_max F.

Using (5) gives `F>=3M/8`. This includes arbitrarily many wholly
excluded fibers among these four: negative upper endpoints were
discarded only in an inequality with the correct direction.

## 4. A wholly captured fiber other than only the rightmost one

A fiber is wholly captured exactly when `l_i>=0`; equality is allowed
because the cap is closed. The central fiber cannot be wholly captured
by (4).

If fiber -1 is wholly captured, its length satisfies

    w_-1=1+2t>=M/4,

since `4(1+2t)-M=2-s+5t>=0` by (2). Its contribution and the
disjoint central contribution B yield

    F>=M/4+Q/(2M)>=3M/8,

where the last inequality uses Cauchy `Q>=M^2/4`.

If fiber 1 is wholly captured, convexity of the lower endpoints gives
`l_2>=2l_1-l_0>0`, so fiber 2 is captured as well. Their combined
length satisfies

    w_1+w_2=1+t>=M/4,

because `4(1+t)-M=2+t-s>=0`. Adding the central contribution and
using the same Cauchy inequality again gives `F>=3M/8`.

These cases include any additional captured fiber on the other end.
The only remaining pattern with any captured fiber has fiber 2 alone
wholly captured.

## 5. Only fiber 2 is wholly captured

Here `D>=t`. Concavity of the upper endpoints gives

    D<=2C-B,
    C>0.

The other three fibers are not wholly captured, and B is positive by
(4). Thus the exact cap mass is

    F=(A)_+ + B + C + t.

Use (3), discard a possibly negative A, and then use `D<=2C-B`:

    Q/2
      <=(1+2t)(A)_+ +sB+C+t(2C-B)
       =(1+2t)[(A)_+ +C]+(s-t)B
      <=K(F-t),

where `K=max(1+2t,s-t)>0`. Consequently

    F>=Q/(2K)+t.                                        (6)

It remains to verify that (6) is at least 3M/8, equivalently
`4Q+8Kt-3KM>=0`. If `K=1+2t`, this difference is

    4s^2-3s-6st+2+3t+18t^2.

It increases with s on (2); at `s=1+t` it equals
`3+2t+16t^2>0`. If `K=s-t`, the difference is

    (s-2)(s-4)+2st+22t+21t^2.

Every term is nonnegative because `1<s<2` and `t>0`. This completes
the last sign pattern and proves (1) for all nonvertical caps through g.

## 6. Vertical halfspaces and closed boundaries

A vertical closed halfspace through the centroid contains either the
indices `0,1,2` or the indices `-1,0`. Their masses are respectively

    s+1+t=(M+s-t)/2>M/2,
    1+2t+s=(M+s+t)/2>M/2.

In particular the entire central boundary fiber has been retained.
Any containing halfspace can be moved parallel inward until its
boundary contains g; the resulting closed halfspace is a subset of
the original and has no larger mass. Nonvertical boundary hyperplanes
meet each interval in at most one point and therefore carry zero
mixed length. All threshold equalities in the captured/excluded cases
above are compatible with these closed-halfspace conventions.

Finally g belongs to C because it is the centroid of a finite positive
measure supported in compact convex C, and its base coordinate is an
integer by hypothesis. Thus g belongs to S; (4) also locates it
strictly inside its positive interval fiber. QED.

## 7. A useful finite-family inequality used by the argument

For any N positive interval fibers with total continuous mean zero,
if the cap `x>=0` wholly captures none of them, then

    cap_mass>=sum w_i^2/(2 max w_i)
             >=M/(1+sqrt(N)).                            (7)

The first inequality is the same exact identity as in Section 3 and
does not need compatibility. To prove the second, let `H=max w_i`
and apply Cauchy to the other N-1 weights. For N>1,

    Q>=H^2+(M-H)^2/(N-1),
    Q/(HM)>=[N(H/M)-2+(M/H)]/(N-1)
             >=2/(1+sqrt(N)).

The final bound follows from `N(H/M)+(M/H)>=2sqrt(N)`.
For N=1 the statement is the ordinary interval midpoint bound.
The four-fiber base balance and width concavity improve (7) from
1/3 to 3/8 via (5). The separately proved concave-weight inequality
of the parent route gives a different improvement for arbitrary N;
no unproved all-N result is used in this four-fiber theorem.
